title: Can, must, want, may
goal: Master the five Danish modal verbs and avoid their biggest trap: *må ikke* means "must not", not "don't have to".
bekal: ask for help and offer help
tell *må ikke*, *skal ikke* and *behøver ikke* apart
wave: Review **unit 11** first: give directions out loud from where you are now to the nearest place you know, using commands.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Flyttedag
dialogs.intro: Budi is moving rooms. Ahmad and Mette come over to help carry his things.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kan I hjælpe mig med sofaen? Den er tung.
lines.id: Can you help me with the sofa? It's heavy.
lines.literal: can you(pl.) help me with sofa-the? it is heavy.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Selvfølgelig. Skal vi tage den ud ad døren først?
lines.id: Of course. Shall we take it out through the door first?
lines.literal: of-course. shall we take it out through door-the first?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Vent — vi må ikke bruge elevatoren til møbler.
lines.id: Wait — we're not allowed to use the elevator for furniture.
lines.literal: wait — we may not use elevator-the for furniture.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Det står i husordenen. Vi skal bruge trappen.
lines.id: It's in the building rules. We have to use the stairs.
lines.literal: it stands in house-order-the. we shall use stairs-the.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Fire etager. Vi bør nok tage en pause undervejs.
lines.id: Four floors. We should probably take a break on the way.
lines.literal: four floors. we ought probably take a pause under-way.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: I behøver ikke bære alt. Jeg kan tage kasserne.
lines.id: You don't have to carry everything. I can take the boxes.
lines.literal: you(pl.) need not carry all. I can take boxes-the.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Vil du have en øl bagefter?
lines.id: Do you want a beer afterwards?
lines.literal: will you have a beer afterwards?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg vil hellere give jer middag. I har hjulpet hele dagen.
lines.id: I'd rather buy you dinner. You've been helping all day.
lines.literal: I will rather give you(pl.) dinner. you(pl.) have helped whole day-the.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Det må du gerne. Men først: sofaen.
lines.id: Sure, go ahead. But first: the sofa.
lines.literal: that may you gladly. but first: sofa-the.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: På tre. En, to, tre — løft!
lines.id: On three. One, two, three — lift!
lines.literal: on three. one, two, three — lift!

notes: **Kan du hjælpe mig?** is the most natural way to ask for help in Danish — far more common than a command. Compare *hjælp mig!*, which sounds like an emergency.
**After a modal verb, the next verb is bare.** *Kan I hjælpe*, not *kan I at hjælpe*. This holds for all five modals without exception — just like English *can help*, never *can to help*.

**Vi må ikke** = we **are not allowed to**. This is the trap. *Må* means "may", so negating it forbids something — even though it looks like English "must". For "don't have to", Danish uses a different word altogether: *behøver ikke*. Choosing wrong here is the difference between "you don't need to pay" and "you're not allowed to pay".
**Det står i husordenen** — *at stå* is used for anything written: *det står i avisen* (it's in the paper), *hvad står der?* (what does it say?). English says "it says", Danish says "it stands".
**Bør nok** — *bør* (should) is softened further with *nok* (probably). Danes love softening advice with little words like these: *nok*, *vist*, *måske*, *lige*, *bare*.
**Jeg vil hellere** = "I'd rather". *Hellere* is the comparative of *gerne*: *gerne → hellere → helst*. So *jeg vil helst* = "what I'd like most".
**Det må du gerne** = "sure, go ahead", literally "that you may gladly". The standard reply to a request for permission, and one of the most typically Danish phrases.
**En etage** is pronounced **uh-TAH-shuh**, from French. Note: the ground floor is called *stuen*, so *første sal* is what Americans call the **second** floor (British: first floor).

grammars.title: The five modal verbs
body: None of the five follow the "stem + -r" pattern, and all five must be memorized. In return, they don't change with the subject either — like every Danish verb.
after: Notice that none of them end in *-r* in the "present" column. That's the quickest way to spot a modal verb in a sentence.

*Må* has two meanings that seem to clash — "may" and "have to" — and context decides. *Må jeg komme ind?* (may I come in?) vs *Jeg må gå nu* (I have to go now). In practice, questions almost always mean "may", statements almost always "have to".
*Skal* also expresses arranged plans, not just obligations: *Jeg skal til tandlægen i morgen* = I have a dentist appointment tomorrow.

grammars.title: Negating modal verbs — the big trap
body: This section is worth reading twice. The meaning of a Danish prohibition is often the opposite of what an English speaker expects.
after: ⚠️ The first two rows cause the most misunderstandings. *Du må ikke betale* means "you're not allowed to pay" — not "you don't have to pay". If you mean the second, say *du behøver ikke betale*.
*Behøver* can be followed by *at* or not — both are accepted. It's the only one on this list that behaves this way, because it's really an ordinary verb, not a full modal.
Prohibition signs in Denmark almost always use this form: *Der må ikke parkeres*, *Man må ikke ryge*. If you see *må ikke* on a sign, it's forbidden.

head: Dansk
English
rows: Kan du gøre mig en tjeneste?
Can you do me a favor?
Do you want to come along?

blocks.text: *At have brug for* = to need. A three-word phrase that can't be shortened: *jeg har brug for hjælp*, *har du brug for noget?*. It's the most common way to say "need" in Danish.
*Godt* in *det kan jeg godt* doesn't mean "good" — it just adds emphasis, like stressed "do" in English ("I *can* do that"). The pattern comes back in *jeg kan godt lide* (I like) in unit 16.

blocks.title: Little softening words
items: **lige** — "quickly, just": *Kan du lige hjælpe mig?* Makes a request sound small and easy to grant.
**nok** — "probably": *Vi bør nok gå.* Softens advice so it doesn't sound preachy.
**vist** — "it seems": *Det er vist for sent.* Leaves room for being wrong.
Danes use these words constantly. A sentence without them sounds blunter than you intend — an impression beginners often make by accident.

sections.title: Modal verbs in questions and negatives

blocks.text: All the word-order rules from unit 10 still apply exactly. The only thing that moves is *ikke*: it comes after the modal verb, before the main verb.

Notice that the main verb (*tale*, *komme*) always stands at the **end**, far from the modal. This will feel more and more natural after unit 19, where the "have done" form takes the same end position.
